t: one who substitutes. One who makes a substitution, saying of an unconsecrated animal that it will be in place of a consecrated animal (for the manner of substitution see below 2:1).
he receives lashes for each and every animal he substitutes. See below halachah 14.
for any negative commandment that involves no act is not punished by lashes etc.. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2.
from swearing. Falsely.
and one who curses his fellow with the Name. Curses using the Name of God or one of the substitute names (ibid. 26:3).
it is impossible that they involve any act at all. They involve speech only.

why is one lashed for substitution, when its prohibition is converted to a positive commandment?. One is not lashed for a negative commandment that comes with an explicit command to rectify the transgression through a particular act, for that command converts ("severs") the prohibition into a positive commandment (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2). Here there is a positive commandment that the substituted animal becomes holy and must be offered.

because it has one positive commandment and two prohibitions. Two prohibitive commands: "He shall not exchange it," and "nor substitute it," and one positive commandment does not override two prohibitions (Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 4b).
for its prohibition is not equivalent to its positive commandment. The prohibition of substitution includes cases where there is no positive commandment when one substitutes.

for the community and partners do not make a substitute if they substituted etc.. The prohibition of substitution applies also to communal offerings and offerings of partners, but when one substitutes in a communal offering or a partners' offering, the substitute does not become holy (see below halachah 12).

even if he substituted on the Sabbath. Although it is forbidden in the first instance to consecrate on the Sabbath, if one consecrated, it is consecrated (Hilchot Shabbat 23:15), and likewise if he substituted on the Sabbath, he is a substituter.
one who intends to say. Of an unconsecrated animal that he owns.

it is a substitute and he receives lashes. Unlike a consecration, where if he intended to say "this is a burnt offering" and said "peace offering," the animal is not consecrated (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:12).

who said: I will enter this house and substitute with my full awareness, and he entered, forgot, and substituted without awareness. He thought of substituting an animal and said that he would enter a house and consider calmly whether to do so, and he entered and forgot his words and substituted without deliberating about it (Rikuy; see there for further explanations).
a person cannot substitute his animal for an offering that is not his. When he says of his unconsecrated animal that it will be in place of his fellow's offering, it is not a substitute.
he substituted for his offering with an animal that is not his. He said of an animal that is not his that it will be in place of his own consecrated animal.

the one who atones makes the substitute, but not the one who consecrates. When one consecrated an offering so that another person would atone through it, the offering belongs to the one who atones, and therefore only he can make a substitute.
the heir. Of a consecrated animal.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 1.
the offerings of gentiles do not make a substitute by Torah law. If a gentile says of an unconsecrated animal that it will be in place of his offering, it is not a substitute.
a gentile consecrated an animal for an Israelite to atone with it, and the gentile substituted for it. For example, where the one atoning gave him permission to substitute (Lechem Mishneh).

it is a doubtful substitute. It is doubtful whether in this case the animal is considered an Israelite's consecrated animal so that it has a substitute by Torah law (Lechem Mishneh, Mirkevet HaMishneh).

a minor who reached the age of vows. A minor who reached the age of thirteen years and one day: his vows count as vows and his consecrations take effect, even though he has not grown two hairs and is not considered an adult for other matters or for lashes (Hilchot Nedarim 11:3-4).

there is doubt whether he makes a substitute or not. The doubt is whether a substitute is like a consecration, which takes effect through a minor, or only an adult who is fit to be lashed can substitute (Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 2b).
priests do not substitute for sin offerings and guilt offerings. Of an Israelite, whose meat they receive.
for they have no claim to the meat until the blood is sprinkled. The priests have no right or permission to eat the meat before the blood is sprinkled.
even though he acquires it from its life. The priest receives the firstborn alive.

he does not acquire it from the start, for its beginning is in an Israelite's house. The firstborn is sanctified from the moment of its birth, and the priest acquires it only after it is given to him.

likewise a priest who substituted for a firstborn born to him... it is a substitute. A firstborn born to a priest is holy and must be offered, and if he substitutes for his firstborn, the law is as for Israelite owners who substituted for a firstborn born in their house.
the high priest's ram makes a substitute. The ram for a burnt offering that he brings from his own on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1), and it is considered an individual's offering.
his bull. The sin-offering bull that the high priest brings from his own (ibid.), which serves to atone for himself, his household and his brother priests.
they are like partners in it. And one does not make a substitute for an animal of partners (above halachah 1).
offerings for the upkeep of the Temple. Those consecrated for the needs of the Temple and not for the altar.
in the tithe. The animal tithe, which is offered on the altar and eaten by its owners.
was not the tithe included in all consecrated things?. And there was no need to prohibit substitution in it specifically.

just as the tithe is an individual's offering. Each individual tithes his animals, and one cannot consecrate and bring a tithe by vow or freewill offering in partnership (Commentary on the Mishnah, Temurah 1:6).
to the grain tithe, which only Israelites are obligated in and not gentiles. Hilchot Terumot 4:15.
this excludes the offerings of gentiles, which do not make a substitute, as we have explained. Above, halachah 6.

one who consecrates an animal with a permanent blemish, it does not make a substitute etc.. An animal with a permanent blemish is not fit for the altar at all, and only its value is consecrated and not its body (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:11), and therefore it cannot make a substitute.

one who consecrates an animal with a transient blemish etc.. When the animal had no permanent blemish at the time of the consecration, its body was consecrated for the altar (ibid.), and therefore even when a permanent blemish later developed in it, it is considered an offering and makes a substitute.

an unblemished animal for a blemished one etc.. Regarding the prohibition of substitution it says: "He shall not exchange it or substitute it, a good for a bad or a bad for a good" (Leviticus 27:10), from which we learn that substitution applies also when one substituted unblemished animals for blemished ones (that were unblemished originally) or blemished for unblemished (Mishnah Temurah 1:2).
a substitute does not make a substitute. When one says of an unconsecrated animal that it will be holy in place of an animal that itself became holy through substitution, it is not consecrated.
the offspring of a consecrated animal. Which is holy by virtue of its mother.
but one who substituted for an animal and then substituted again. For the same animal, in such a way that all the substitutions were for the directly consecrated animal.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 14.

one who substitutes for a mixed-breed or a treifah etc.. All of these are unfit for offering on the altar (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:3-4 and the commentary there). If he said of one animal that it will be in place of a consecrated animal, it is not consecrated. Likewise, if one of them was consecrated and he said of an unblemished animal that it be holy in its place, it is not a substitute (Commentary on the Mishnah, Temurah 2:3).

a blemished animal whose species has an offering etc.. This kind of animal is offered. But mixed-breeds, the tumtum and the androgynos are kinds that are not offered at all (see also there halachah 10; and treifah too has no sanctity at all since it is forbidden to eat, Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 17a).
one who copulates and one who is copulated with. An animal that had relations with a person or that a person had relations with, and is unfit for offering.
they are like a blemished animal. See Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:10.
and likewise anything similar. Such as an animal set aside for idolatry or worshiped as an idol (see there).
an animal that is half sacred and half unconsecrated. An animal of two partners, one of whom consecrated his share (Rikuy).
does not make a substitute. When he said of an unconsecrated animal that it will be in its place.
and it does not become a substitute. When he said that it will be in place of a consecrated animal.

all sin offerings whose law is that they die. For example, the offspring of a sin offering and a sin offering whose owner died, whose law is to die, and they cannot be offered or redeemed (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1).
a sin offering whose law is that it grazes until it develops a blemish and is sold. After the sale its proceeds fall to freewill offerings, such as a sin offering that passed its year (ibid. 5:7).
one who sets aside a female for his Passover offering, burnt offering or guilt offering. These offerings come only from males.

since they descended to the sanctity of value, and they are unblemished, they descend to the sanctity of the body. Since they were consecrated, even though they are not fit for the offering for which they were consecrated, because they are unblemished and generally fit to be an offering, the sanctity of the body applies to them (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:16), and therefore they make a substitute.
one who sets aside a male goat for his sin offering. An individual's sin offering comes as a female.
a nasi who set aside a female goat for his sin offering. A nasi's sin offering comes as a male.
a high priest who set aside a cow for his sin offering. And not a bull, as he is obligated.
as we have explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 4:18.
this is in place of that. And likewise if he said "this is the substitute of that" (see above 1:2).
in place of this... the exchange of this. When the consecrated animal is before him.
this is in place of a burnt offering... he has said nothing. Since he did not refer to a specific consecrated animal.

this is desecrated on that, it is not a substitute. The language of desecration is not the language of substitution but of releasing a consecrated item to unconsecrated status, and in the case of an unblemished consecrated animal (which cannot be released to unconsecrated status) it has no effect at all.

he placed his hand on an unconsecrated animal and said "this is in place of that," it is a substitute etc.. The expression "in place of this" is used both for substitution and for desecration (Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 27a). Therefore, when he placed his hand on the unconsecrated animal, it is evident that he intended it to become consecrated with the sanctity of the consecrated animal, whereas when he places his hand on the consecrated animal, it is evident that he intended it to be desecrated onto the unconsecrated animal (since the animal is already holy).

if two unconsecrated animals in place of the two unblemished ones, they are their substitutes and he is lashed twice. Unblemished animals cannot be desecrated, and regarding them there is no doubt that he intended substitution.

he intended to desecrate it and not to substitute, since he has a permitted way before him etc.. Since for one of the animals there is a possibility that his statement was made in a permitted manner, we assume he prefers this possibility (and all the more so where there was only one blemished consecrated animal, where he may not have transgressed any prohibition, we say that he intended desecration and is not lashed - see Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 27a).
there is a presumption that a person does not leave the permitted and do the forbidden. For this principle see also Hilchot Shechitah 4:15, Hilchot Shemittah 9:26.

for even though this man was presumed to have incurred many lashes. Even though this person certainly transgressed nine prohibitions for which lashes are due, we say of him that he does not leave the permitted and do the forbidden.

and a blemished animal is desecrated onto a blemished animal, for he does not leave the permitted and do the forbidden. Therefore we do not say that he intended to substitute the unblemished for the blemished and the blemished for the unblemished.
his words stand. Half of it becomes the substitute for a burnt offering and half the substitute for a peace offering.
and it is sold. After a blemish develops in it, since one cannot offer half a burnt offering and half a peace offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:3).

if he intended this from the start, his words stand. If from the outset he intended to substitute half for a burnt offering and half for a peace offering, the law is as in the case where he said "the substitute of a burnt offering and peace offering."

within the time of speaking. The length of time it takes to say "Peace upon you, Rabbi" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17). Generally, retracting within the time of speaking cancels the earlier statement, but in consecration this rule does not apply (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:1).
and if its substitute was a female. And a female cannot be offered as a burnt offering.
the female grazes until it develops a blemish and is sold. And once blemished it is sold immediately.
the substitute of a sin offering dies, as we have explained in Pesulei HaMukdashin. 4:1.
and its proceeds fall to freewill offerings. The money is placed in the chests from which communal freewill burnt offerings are brought (see below 4:5).
requires semichah. Leaning on the animal's head before slaughtering it.
and libations. Fine flour mixed with oil, and wine, that accompany the offering.
and waving of the breast and thigh. After flaying and dissecting the peace offering, the priest and the owner wave the breast and thigh together with the emurim.
except that it does not require bread, as we have explained in Pesulei HaMukdashin. 12:8.
if he substituted for it before midday of the fourteenth. Before the proper time for offering.

its substitute is not offered but grazes until it develops a blemish. Since he substituted at a time when the offering was not yet fit to be offered, the substitute cannot be offered (Rikuy, Mirkevet HaMishneh).
and if he substituted for it after midday. At the time of offering the Passover offering, before he offered his Passover.
the substitute itself is offered as a peace offering. Since only one animal can be offered as the Passover offering, the substitute is offered as a peace offering.
and the law of the tithe is like the firstborn. We learn the tithe from the laws of the firstborn by gezerah shavah (Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 5b).
the substitute of a firstborn goes to the priests. Like the firstborn itself.
and the substitute of the tithe goes to the owners. Like the tithe itself.
just as a firstborn and tithe that developed a blemish are not redeemed. Rather, they are eaten without redemption.
as we have explained in Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach. 1:12.

an animal he consecrated half as a burnt offering and half as a peace offering. Its law is that it grazes until it develops a blemish and is sold, and with half its proceeds he brings a burnt offering and with half a peace offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:3).
and likewise any consecrated animal that is not offered because of its original consecration. For example, a female consecrated as a burnt offering.

half of this animal is a substitute and half a burnt offering, it is offered as a burnt offering. Since only a whole animal can be substituted for (above 1:16), the substitution does not take effect and the whole animal is consecrated as a burnt offering (Rikuy).

half a burnt offering and half a tithe, it is offered as a burnt offering. Since one cannot consecrate half an animal as a tithe, the whole animal is a burnt offering (Or Sameach; and this applies even if he consecrated it while the animals were passing under the rod, when the sanctity of a tithe could have taken effect on the animal).

half a substitute and half a tithe, it is doubtful and is not offered. Since there is no substitution for half an animal and no tithe for half an animal, it is doubtful which designation takes precedence (Or Sameach).
one who consecrates an animal with a transient blemish, and needless to say an unblemished one. And the sanctity of the body took effect on them.

and afterward a permanent blemish developed and it was redeemed etc.. After redemption, the meat may be eaten as unconsecrated food, but with regard to several matters (such as the prohibition of shearing and working) the animal retains its sanctity (see Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9). And with regard to substitution too it retains its sanctity and makes a substitute.
it is not offered because it came from a displaced sanctity. Its sanctity came from an animal that was redeemed and no longer has the sanctity of the body.
and it is not redeemed, for its sanctity lacks the power to take hold of its redemption. Its sanctity is weak and cannot attach to the redemption money.

all substitutes that were permanently blemished from the start. An animal with a permanent blemish that was substituted for a consecrated animal: the substitution takes effect and it becomes consecrated (above 1:14).

and they do not go out to unconsecrated status for all purposes, so that they would be permitted to be sheared and worked after their redemption. When one consecrates an animal with a permanent blemish, the sanctity of the body does not take effect on it and after redemption it is permitted to be sheared and worked (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9). But if he substituted it for a consecrated animal, the sanctity of the body takes effect and it is not permitted to be sheared and worked after redemption.
he brings another sacrifice from his house. An unconsecrated animal fit for sacrifice.

if this is a substitute of a substitute, then the one he brought is unconsecrated. He stipulates that if the substitute animal is unconsecrated (a substitute of a substitute), then the animal he brought from his house also remains unconsecrated.

and if it is the substitute of a burnt offering or peace offering, then the one he brought is a burnt offering or peace offering. He continues to stipulate that if the substitute is the substitute of the other animal that was consecrated, he consecrates the animal he brought from his house: if the substitute is a substitute of a burnt offering, he consecrates the one he brought as a peace offering, and if it is a substitute of a peace offering, he consecrates the one he brought as a burnt offering (Rikuy, Lechem Mishneh).

the one he brought with the second substitute is like a sacrifice and substitute that became mixed up. After he brought the animal from his house and consecrated it under the stated conditions, it turns out that possibly both animals are unconsecrated, or possibly one is a burnt offering and the other a peace offering. Their law is as in the case mentioned in the previous paragraph of a sacrifice and a substitute that were mixed together, which are treated as a mixture of a burnt offering and a peace offering (Lechem Mishneh).
and we have already explained the law of mixtures in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 6:6.
in sacrifices. In peace offerings.

like a burnt offering and peace offering that were mixed together. One must wait until both develop a blemish, and he buys with the proceeds of the better one a burnt offering and a peace offering (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 6:6).

he substituted again for one of the two and it is not known which one he substituted for. If he substituted for the substitute animal, that animal is unconsecrated, since a substitute does not make a substitute (above 1:15), and if he substituted for the animal he had consecrated, that animal is consecrated and it is not known whether it is a burnt offering or a peace offering.
a firstborn or a tithe. Whose substitutes are neither offered nor redeemed.
and he substituted for one of them, it is not offered. Lest it be the substitute of a firstborn or tithe.

but grazes until it develops a blemish and is eaten like a firstborn or a tithe. After it develops a blemish he brings another animal and redeems the substitute with it, in case it is the substitute of a peace offering, and then he eats it by the law of a firstborn or tithe.
as we have explained. Above, halachot 1-2 (for a similar law regarding a mixture of a firstborn and tithe among consecrated animals see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 6:14).

they are like peace offerings, and they themselves are peace offerings for all purposes. The offspring of a peace offering and the offspring of the substitute of a peace offering have the sanctity of peace offerings, and they themselves are offered as peace offerings.
except that they do not require bread... as we have explained. Above 3:1.

for from his actions it is evident that he is delaying them in order to raise herds upon herds from them. From the man's actions, that he did not offer the offspring but kept them until offspring were born from them, it appears that he wants to have many peace offering animals (whose meat is eaten). Since this involves the prohibition of bal te'acher (delaying), they penalize him (Commentary on the Mishnah, Temurah 3:1).
the offspring of a sin offering dies. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1.
and needless to say the offspring of its substitute. For its mother (the substitute of a sin offering) also dies (above 3:1).

and he found in it a living four-month fetus. A live fetus whose months of gestation have not been completed, which is considered one of its mother's limbs and is made permissible to eat by her slaughter (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 5:14), and therefore is not considered the offspring of a sin offering, which must die.
it is eaten like the meat of the sin offering. On the day of slaughter and the night after until midnight, in the Temple courtyard, by male priests (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:19).

for the offspring of consecrated animals are consecrated while in their mothers' wombs. Therefore the sanctity of a sin offering applies to the fetus (unlike a firstborn, which is sanctified only at birth, as below halachot 12-13).

the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering. A guilt offering comes only from males, and so only with the substitute of a guilt offering (when it is female) can there be an offspring that is offered on the altar.

and if it gave birth to a male after he offered his guilt offering, the offspring itself is offered as a burnt offering. When it was born before he offered his guilt offering, the offspring is not offered as a burnt offering, lest people err and offer it as the guilt offering, and so its proceeds fall to freewill offerings. But after the guilt offering was offered, when there is no concern that they will offer the offspring in place of the guilt offering, it may be offered as a burnt offering (Rikuy).
he set aside a female for his guilt offering and it gave birth, it and its offspring graze until they develop a blemish etc.. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:16.
we have already explained in Ma'aseh HaKorbanot that wherever etc.. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:7.

that he give the money to the shofarot that were in the Temple, whose number in shekels we have explained. Six of the thirteen chests ("shofarot") in the Temple were designated for communal freewill burnt offerings (Hilchot Shekalim 2:2-3).
it requires semichah and its libations come from his own. Like any individual's burnt offering.
. In the printed editions the order of the next two halachot was switched, but in the manuscripts it is as here.

the offspring of the substitute of a burnt offering. An animal burnt offering comes only from males, so only with the substitute of a burnt offering (when it is female) can there be an offspring that is offered on the altar.
and the offspring of its offspring forever. With a burnt offering they did not decree lest he raise herds upon herds, since the owners do not benefit from its meat (Lechem Mishneh above, halachah 1).
one who set aside a female for his burnt offering. Its law is that it grazes until it develops a blemish and he brings a male burnt offering with its proceeds.

even though it gave birth to a male, it grazes until it develops a blemish. Since it was sanctified by virtue of its mother, and she cannot be offered, he too is not offered (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:17).
the offspring of the substitute of a firstborn go to the priest. Like the firstborn itself (see above 3:2).
and the offspring of a tithe and its substitute belong to its owners. Like the tithe itself.
if its mother was offered as a peace offering. Where he substituted for it after midday of the fourteenth of Nisan, which is the beginning of the time for offering the Passover.
and if its law was that it be sold and he bring a peace offering with its proceeds. Where he substituted for it before midday, before the time of offering the Passover (above 3:1).

one who set aside a female for his Passover offering. The Passover offering comes only from males, and its law is that it grazes until it develops a blemish and he brings a Passover offering with its proceeds, and if it did not develop a blemish until he offered his Passover, he brings a peace offering with its proceeds (Hilchot Korban Pesach 4:4). The law of its offspring is the same.

by way of Dofen, or if they gave birth to a tumtum, androgynos, mixed-breed or treifah. Which are not fit for the altar and whose bodies do not become consecrated (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:10), and therefore he can redeem them without a blemish.

the offspring of a blemished animal is like the offspring of an unblemished one. Since the mother was originally fit for the altar, her offspring is offered (this refers to an animal consecrated before a permanent blemish developed in it; but if it was consecrated after it already had a permanent blemish, the offspring is redeemed and goes out to unconsecrated status, Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:11).
afterbirth. The membrane in which the fetus is contained.
and they are forbidden for benefit. Like all that must be buried (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:13).

one who changes consecrated things from one sanctity to another. One who consecrates a consecrated item to a different sanctity, which is forbidden even though once it was consecrated to one sanctity, the consecration he makes to another sanctity has no effect.

things consecrated for the upkeep of the Temple. Those consecrated for the needs and maintenance of the Temple; if he consecrated them for a specific item in the upkeep of the Temple, he cannot change them to another item.
how does one use a stratagem etc.. In what manner can one find a permitted stratagem to remove from the firstborn its sanctity as a firstborn and transfer it to another sanctity.
he may say. He is permitted to say.
and if he said, upon the emergence of most of its head. The emergence of most of the head counts as birth, and after it one can no longer consecrate the firstborn to another sanctity.

rather it has the sanctity of its mother. Even if they consecrate it to another sanctity it remains with its mother's sanctity, like consecrated animals that have been born, where a change does not alter their sanctity.
for the offspring of consecrated animals are consecrated in their mothers' wombs, as we have explained. Above, halachah 3.
as we have explained at the end of Me'ilah. Hilchot Me'ilah 8:8.

for what the verse says: "it and its substitute shall be holy," corresponds to what it says: "and if the one who consecrates etc.". The reason for the law that the substitute becomes holy is the same as the reason for which the Torah commanded that one who redeems his property from consecration add a fifth to its value (Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 4:5).
Have I not written to you three times?. A name for the Torah.
